doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Learning to compose and arrange
summary: Piano is only a writer's tool for her; she first wrote a percussion and sax suite for Al Hamme, and now studies Brookmeyer and Thad Jones and writes with Tommy Newsom.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well the whole other side of your career, a part of it is as a composer. When you started composing did you find a need to have keyboard skills? Or usually we think of a drummer, unless they go out of their way to get all the harmony study, as maybe not having that as much.

Yeah well you have to, it’s a requirement in school, to learn how to play the piano. How when you go into a jazz program you have to take jazz piano as well. But I mean I’m horrible, I can’t play the piano, but I can play it as a writer. You know I can figure out my own chords and I can play through a passage like in slow motion until I learn it. And certainly I’ve studied harmony and theory, like inside out, enough to make you sick. But you know I started writing and this is also funny. Al Hamme, the person from Binghamton, he took me to — he was playing at some saxophone workshop or something like that. And it was like I’ll go. He said, “I’m playing this new music.” So I went to hear

the concert. And I went to several performances that day. And I could not stand any of it. And this is how stupid I was. I said, “that music is so horrible, I bet I could write something better than that.” So the first thing I wrote was this four movement suite for percussion and saxophone for Al. And we played it and it came out really good. So I was like well I can kind of do this too. I don’t mean it to sound, like that sounds like egomaniacal, but for some reason, I don’t mean it that way. I just was thinking, jeez, even I could try something better than this. And it could have been boom-chick boom-chick and I probably would have liked it better. But it came out that doing jazz composition and arranging is never, ever, ever ending study. To me it’s so complicated, it’s very sophisticated and there’s so many high standards and people to idolize as writers. Somebody that I love, Tommy Newsom is a great writer, writes a lot for my band and I’m so blessed to have him.

Yeah. And the things you can study now in arranging with Bob Brookmeyer’s music and Thad Jones, and that again is the other thing where it’s all, those guys just invented what they did. And for me I just go to a book and go oh, here’s Thad Jones’ voicing on the G7 chord. Okay, I’ll steal that. So I don’t have to think as hard as they did. I can just steal things from the books.
